# How to Use This Guide

The fretboard is a grid. Learn a few **geometric facts** (how intervals look
between strings) and chords and progressions stop being shapes to memorize.
They become moves you can work out anywhere on the neck.

Each lesson is short: an idea, how it looks on the neck, an interactive
fretboard, and something to **try**. All figures play sound. In chord diagrams
the dots are labelled by **degree** (R = root, 3, 5, ♭7, …), colored the same
way throughout. When a progression plays, a **gold ring** marks a note that
stays put and an **orange line** marks a note that moves by a step.

Standard tuning (E A D G B E). High E is drawn at the top. Tick
*⚙ low E on top* on any fretboard to flip them all.

# Part I · Fretboard Geometry

## Lesson 1 · Strings are a fourth apart, except one

Neighbouring strings are a **perfect 4th** (5 frets) apart, except **G → B**,
which is a **major 3rd** (4 frets).

**The B-string rule:** any shape that crosses from G to B moves **one fret
higher** on the far side. Every "exception" in guitar geometry is this rule.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="string-intervals"}
[Interactive figure: interval shapes walking across the strings, showing the B-string shift. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

**Try:** pick *Octave* and walk it across the strings. Notice the jump from +2
to +3 frets.

## Lesson 2 · Interval shapes

From a note to a higher (thinner) string:

| Interval | Shape | Crossing G→B |
|---|---|---|
| Perfect 4th | next string, **same fret** | +1 |
| Perfect 5th | next string, **+2** | +3 |
| Major 3rd | next string, **−1** | same fret |
| Minor 3rd | next string, **−2** | −1 |
| Octave | skip a string, **+2** | **+3** |
| Minor 10th | three strings over, **same fret** | +1 |
| Major 10th | three strings over, **+1** | **+2** |

The 10ths (a 3rd plus an octave) give the wide, open sound of riffs like
*Road Trippin'*. From A→B and D→high E the B string adds a fret, which is why
those shapes are "one or two frets forward".

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="interval-finder"}
[Interactive figure: click a fret to see its octaves, 5ths, 4ths, 3rds and 10ths. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

**Try:** click a note on the A string, then find its octave on the G string
and its major 10th on the B string without looking.

## Lesson 3 · One string over = a resolution

Moving a root to the **next string at the same fret** raises it a 4th, which
is the same note as a 5th lower. That is the root motion of **V → I**. Keep
going and you walk the circle of fifths, alternating between 6th-string and
5th-string shapes and drifting two frets down every two chords.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-chords="G C F B♭ E♭" data-position="3" data-note="Dashed grey line: root motion. Every step is up a 4th (= down a 5th)."}
[Interactive figure: roots walking around the circle of fifths across the strings. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

# Part II · Orientation

## Lesson 4 · Where the chords of a key live

Find the tonic, and the other chords sit in a fixed pattern around it:

- **I, IV, V** make an **L** across two strings.
- **ii and vi** sit two frets above I and V.
- **vi** (the relative minor) is **3 frets below** the tonic on the same string.
- With the tonic on the 5th string, **V is directly above it** on the 6th string, same fret.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="key-map"}
[Interactive figure: the diatonic chords of a key laid out on the neck. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

**Try:** pick a key, close your eyes, find I–vi–IV–V, then check.

# Part III · Building Chords

## Lesson 5 · One note, three roles

Any note can be the **root**, the **3rd** or the **5th** of a chord, and each
of those can be major or minor. That gives six chords for every melody note.
For C: C and Cm (root), A♭ and Am (3rd), F and Fm (5th).

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="chord-roles"}
[Interactive figure: pick a note and its role to see the chord built around it. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

**Try:** pick a note on the high E string and harmonize it all six ways
without moving your hand more than a few frets.

## Lesson 6 · The same chord in five places (CAGED)

Every major or minor chord can be played with the shape of an open **C, A, G,
E or D** chord moved up the neck. The five shapes interlock: the top of one is
the bottom of the next.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="caged"}
[Interactive figure: one chord in its five CAGED positions. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

**Try:** play one chord in all five positions going up the neck, then come back down.

# Part IV · Chord Vocabulary

## Lesson 7 · Seventh chords

Add a 7th to a triad and you get the chords that drive functional harmony:

| Chord | Formula | Role |
|---|---|---|
| maj7 | 1 3 5 7 | restful I and IV |
| 7 (dominant) | 1 3 5 ♭7 | tension that wants to resolve |
| m7 | 1 ♭3 5 ♭7 | ii, iii, vi |
| m7♭5 (ø7) | 1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7 | vii in major, ii in minor |
| °7 | 1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭♭7 | a leading-tone chord (Lesson 10) |

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="chord-shapes" data-qualities="maj7,7,m7,m7b5,dim7"}
[Interactive figure: seventh-chord shapes with the root on the 6th or 5th string. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## Lesson 8 · Shells and guide tones

The **3rd and 7th** carry a seventh chord's identity, and the 5th adds little.
A **shell** voicing keeps just root, 3rd and 7th: three notes, easy to move.

In **ii–V–I**, the guide tones barely move: each chord's **7th falls a half
step** to the next chord's **3rd** while the other guide tone holds.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-voicing="shell" data-shells="toggle" data-presets="Major = Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 | ii7 V7 Imaj7 | C (7th of Dm7) falls to B (3rd of G7), then F (7th of G7) falls to E (3rd of Cmaj7).; Minor = Dm7b5 G7 Cm7 | iiø7 V7 i7 | The same guide-tone motion in minor."}
[Interactive figure: ii–V–I in shell voicings, showing the guide-tone motion. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

**Try:** switch between *Full* and *Shell*. Play the shells while a friend
(or a looper) plays the roots.

## Lesson 9 · Suspended chords

A **sus4** swaps the 3rd for the 4th (a **sus2** for the 2nd). With no 3rd,
the chord is neither major nor minor, and it wants to settle.

- **Vsus4 → V → I** delays the leading tone.
- **V7 → Isus4 → I** is the classic **4–3 suspension**. The 7th of V7 (F in
  G7) is *held* into the tonic as its 4th, then falls to the 3rd.
- In minor, the sus chord can land on **i**, or on a major **I** for a bright
  ending: the **Picardy third**.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-presets="4–3 suspension = G7 Csus4 C | V7 Isus4 I | F is held from G7 into Csus4, then falls to E.; Vsus4 → V → I = C Gsus4 G C | I Vsus4 V I | The 4th (C) falls to the 3rd (B), which then rises to the tonic.; Minor, then Picardy = Cm G7 Csus4 Cm G7 Csus4 C | i V7 isus4 i V7 isus4 I | Same suspension, but the second time it resolves to C major."}
[Interactive figure: suspended chords resolving. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## Lesson 10 · Symmetric chords: diminished and augmented

The **diminished triad** sits on vii in major and ii in minor. **B° is G7
without its G**, so it works as a dominant.

The **diminished 7th** is stacked minor thirds, so it is symmetric: **slide it
3 frets and you get the same four notes** in a new order. Any of those notes
can be a leading tone, so **one shape resolves to four keys**.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="symmetric" data-type="dim7"}
[Interactive figure: a diminished 7th sliding in 3-fret steps, with its four resolutions. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

The **augmented** triad is stacked major thirds: it repeats every **4 frets**,
and as a V+ (G B D♯) its raised 5th pushes up to the tonic's 3rd. It resolves
three ways.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="symmetric" data-type="aug"}
[Interactive figure: an augmented triad sliding in 4-fret steps, with its three resolutions. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

# Part V · Function: Progressions That Move

## Lesson 11 · Cadences: I, IV and V

The three primary chords, and four ways a phrase can end:

- **Authentic** V → I: the strongest close.
- **Plagal** IV → I: the softer "amen".
- **Deceptive** V → vi: you expect I and get its relative minor.
- **Half cadence**: ending *on* V, which leaves the phrase open.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-position="3" data-presets="Authentic = C F G7 C | I IV V7 I; Plagal = C F C | I IV I; Deceptive = C F G7 Am | I IV V7 vi; Half = C Am F G | I vi IV V"}
[Interactive figure: the four cadences. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## Lesson 12 · ii – V – I and its relatives

The core progression of functional harmony, and the variations worth knowing:

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-presets="ii–V–I = Dm G C | ii V I; With 7ths = Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 | ii7 V7 Imaj7; II–V–I = D7 G7 C | V7/V V7 I | ii made major: D7 is the V of V, a secondary dominant (Lesson 13).; Minor = Dm7b5 G7 Cm | iiø7 V7 i | In minor, ii is half-diminished.; Neapolitan = D♭ G7 Cm | ♭II V7 i | ♭II is a major triad on the lowered 2nd, usually played with F in the bass (N6)."}
[Interactive figure: ii–V–I variations. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Your notes, checked
- *"ii7 > V > i"*: in minor, ii is naturally **half-diminished** (iiø7 = Dm7♭5).
- *"iib7 > V > i (Neapolitan)"*: the Neapolitan is **♭II**, a major triad on
  the lowered 2nd (D♭ F A♭ in C minor). It is not a 7th chord.
:::

## Lesson 13 · Secondary dominants

Any chord can be approached by **its own V7**. II–V–I (Lesson 12) and the
I → I7 → IV move (Lesson 21) are two cases of one rule. Each secondary
dominant adds a note from outside the key that leads into its target: G♯ → A,
C♯ → D, F♯ → G.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-position="3" data-presets="V7/vi = C E7 Am | I V7/vi vi | E7 is the III chord made dominant (see Lesson 16).; V7/ii = C A7 Dm | I V7/ii ii; V7/IV = C C7 F | I V7/IV IV; V7/V = C D7 G | I V7/V V; Chain = C E7 Am A7 Dm D7 G7 C | I V7/vi vi V7/ii ii V7/V V7 I | Every chord is preceded by its own dominant."}
[Interactive figure: secondary dominants. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## Lesson 14 · Tritone substitution

G7 and **D♭7** share the same two guide tones: **B (= C♭) and F**, the
tritone that makes a dominant restless. So D♭7 can replace G7. The bass then
slides **down a half step** into the tonic instead of falling a fifth.

On the neck, the substitute is the same 7th shape **6 frets away**.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-voicing="shell" data-shells="toggle" data-presets="V7 → I = Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 | ii7 V7 Imaj7; Tritone sub = Dm7 D♭7 Cmaj7 | ii7 ♭II7 Imaj7 | The guide tones are the same as in G7, only the root changes."}
[Interactive figure: a ii–V–I with and without the tritone substitute. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## Lesson 15 · Circles of fifths

Root motion **down a fifth** is the strongest move in tonal harmony. Chain it
and you get long progressions that pull steadily home. On the neck it is
Lesson 3 again: one string over, same fret.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-position="5" data-presets="Triads = Em Am Dm G C | iii vi ii V I; Sevenths = Em7 Am7 Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 | iii7 vi7 ii7 V7 Imaj7; All dominants = E7 A7 D7 G7 C | V7/vi V7/ii V7/V V7 I | Every chord is the dominant of the next."}
[Interactive figure: circle-of-fifths progressions. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## Lesson 16 · Mediant moves: keep the tonic's quality

The chords on the 3rd and 6th degrees normally have the **opposite quality**
to the tonic: iii and vi are minor in major, III and VI are major in minor.
**Keep the tonic's quality instead** and you get a *chromatic mediant*.

| Move | Diatonic (2 common tones) | Mediant (1 common tone) |
|---|---|---|
| I → III | C → Em | **C → E** |
| I → VI | C → Am | **C → A** |
| i → ♭iii | Cm → E♭ | **Cm → E♭m** |
| i → ♭vi | Cm → A♭ | **Cm → A♭m** |

One note stays and two move by step, so the move is smooth. But the new notes
come from outside the key, which gives a bright, cinematic lift. In major,
III and VI also work as secondary dominants (Lesson 13). **On the neck: keep
the barre shape and slide it** (+4 or −3 frets in major, +3 or −4 in minor).

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-position="5" data-presets="Major, diatonic = C Em C Am C | I iii I vi I; Major, mediants = C E C A C | I III I VI I; Minor, diatonic = Cm E♭ Cm A♭ Cm | i III i VI i; Minor, mediants = Cm E♭m Cm A♭m Cm | i ♭iii i ♭vi i"}
[Interactive figure: diatonic and chromatic mediant moves. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

**Try:** play the diatonic preset, then the mediant one, and listen for the moment the music "lifts".

## Lesson 17 · Borrowed chords

Borrow chords from the **parallel minor** (C minor's chords in C major) and a
major key gets darker colors:

- **iv** (Fm): the A♭ sighs down to G. This is the "minor plagal" cadence.
- **♭VII** (B♭): a rock and Mixolydian sound, I → ♭VII → IV → I.
- **♭VI → ♭VII → I** (A♭ → B♭ → C): a triumphant cadence, the shape sliding up in whole steps.
- **V → ♭VI**: a deceptive cadence that also borrows (compare Lesson 11).

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-position="3" data-presets="iv = C F Fm C | I IV iv I | A (in F) sighs to A♭ (in Fm), then to G.; ♭VII = C B♭ F C | I ♭VII IV I; ♭VI–♭VII–I = C A♭ B♭ C | I ♭VI ♭VII I; V → ♭VI = C G7 A♭ | I V7 ♭VI"}
[Interactive figure: borrowed chords. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

# Part VI · Idioms

## Lesson 18 · Line clichés

Hold a chord and move **one inner voice chromatically**: one finger walks
while everything else stays. Over a minor chord the line descends
(A → G♯ → G → F♯). Over a major chord it climbs (G → G♯ → A → B♭).

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-presets="Minor = Am@x07555 Ammaj7@x06555 Am7@x05555 Am6@x04555 | i i(maj7) i7 i6 | The line is on the D string: A, G♯, G, F♯.; Major = C@x32010 Caug@x32110 C6@x32210 C7@x32310 | I I+ I6 I7 | The line is on the G string: G, G♯, A, B♭. C7 then wants to go to F."}
[Interactive figure: line clichés over a minor and a major chord. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## Lesson 19 · The 12-bar blues

The blues breaks the rules on purpose: **every chord is a dominant 7th**, even
the tonic. Twelve bars, three chords:

| I7 | I7 | I7 | I7 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **IV7** | **IV7** | **I7** | **I7** |
| **V7** | **IV7** | **I7** | **V7** |

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-position="5" data-loop="" data-speed="1.0" data-chords="A7 A7 A7 A7 D7 D7 A7 A7 E7 D7 A7 E7" data-labels="I7 I7 I7 I7 IV7 IV7 I7 I7 V7 IV7 I7 V7" data-note="The last bar (V7) is the turnaround back to the top."}
[Interactive figure: a 12-bar blues in A. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## Lesson 20 · The Andalusian cadence

**i → ♭VII → ♭VI → V** (Am → G → F → E): a bass line stepping down the minor
scale, ending on a **major** V borrowed from harmonic minor. Its G♯ pulls
back to A. On the neck it is the same barre shape stepping down, the sound of
flamenco.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-position="5" data-loop="" data-chords="Am G F E" data-labels="i ♭VII ♭VI V"}
[Interactive figure: the Andalusian cadence. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

# Part VII · Exercises

## Lesson 21 · The dominant chain

1. Play **V7 → I** (G7 → C).
2. Turn the I into a dominant 7th (C → **C7**). It is now the V7 of **IV**.
3. Resolve (C7 → F), and repeat: F → F7 → B♭ → B♭7 → …
4. After twelve keys you are back home.

The roots alternate between the 6th and 5th strings (Lesson 3).

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="progression" data-position="3" data-speed="1.0" data-chords="G7 C C7 F F7 B♭ B♭7 E♭ E♭7 A♭ A♭7 D♭ D♭7 G♭ G♭7 B B7 E E7 A A7 D D7 G" data-labels="V7 I V7 I V7 I V7 I V7 I V7 I V7 I V7 I V7 I V7 I V7 I"}
[Interactive figure: the dominant chain through all twelve keys. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::
